congress.rationale: Largest single buy in a broad international-equity spree; defense names benefit from sustained European and NATO rearmament budgets.
congress.deepDive: BAE Systems was the biggest single ticket in a same-day basket of ~12 international names, signalling it as the highest-conviction line. The thesis rests on multi-year European and NATO defense spending commitments (most members now at or above 2% of GDP) that give primes like BAE a long, visible order backlog. Harman previously chaired/served on national-security bodies, so defense exposure fits her domain. Practically this reads as a structural tailwind trade rather than a tactical punt — relevant to your own WisdomTree/iShares defense thesis even though you don't hold BAE directly.

congress.rationale: Amadeus IT, a travel-tech platform; sized larger than peers, consistent with a bet on durable global travel demand.
congress.deepDive: Amadeus runs the GDS rails behind airline and hotel bookings, so it's a toll-road on global travel volumes rather than a bet on any single carrier. Sized in the top tier of the basket, it implies confidence that post-pandemic travel demand is structural, not a one-off rebound, and that airlines keep outsourcing distribution tech. It's a quality-compounder profile (high margins, recurring transaction fees) that pairs with the rest of her dividend/blue-chip adds. The risk is a global travel slowdown or carriers in-housing distribution.

congress.rationale: Ferrari; part of a diversified European blue-chip / luxury basket added the same day.
congress.deepDive: Ferrari is the purest pricing-power name in luxury — a multi-year order book and deliberate supply scarcity insulate it from demand wobbles that hit mass luxury. As a smaller line in the basket it looks like diversification into resilient high-end consumer rather than a core bet. The read-through is a tilt toward 'quality at any cycle' European consumer names. Main risk is luxury cyclicality and FX (euro earnings).

congress.rationale: International bank exposure; high-dividend financials added alongside Barclays in the same session.
congress.deepDive: HSBC is an Asia-weighted global bank with a fat dividend and ongoing buybacks, fitting an income-oriented international sleeve. Buying it alongside Barclays the same day shows a deliberate add of rate-sensitive financials rather than a single-name call. The thesis benefits from still-elevated net interest margins and capital returns. Watch points: China/HK property exposure and any sharp rate-cut cycle compressing margins — directly relevant to your own DBS/SGX-bank weighting.

congress.rationale: Barclays; UK financials add complements the HSBC purchase, leaning into rate-sensitive income.
congress.deepDive: Barclays pairs a UK retail bank with an investment bank that re-rates when trading and capital-markets activity recover. Trading near tangible book with an active buyback, it's a classic value-financial. Bought beside HSBC, it confirms a thematic 'cheap international banks with capital returns' add. The IB exposure makes earnings lumpier than a pure retail bank, so it carries more cyclicality than the HSBC line.

congress.rationale: Diageo; defensive consumer-staples/spirits name typical of a yield-oriented international allocation.
congress.deepDive: Diageo (Johnnie Walker, Guinness, Don Julio) is a defensive staples compounder leaning on premiumization and brand pricing power. The stock had de-rated on soft US spirits demand and destocking, so this looks like a value entry into a beaten-down quality name. It adds ballast and yield to the basket. The risk is that the spirits slowdown proves structural (younger cohorts drinking less) rather than cyclical.

congress.rationale: GSK; defensive UK pharma added as part of the diversified dividend basket.
congress.deepDive: GSK offers defensive pharma cash flows, a vaccines franchise, and a recovering pipeline at a discount to US peers. As a small basket line it adds healthcare defensiveness and yield rather than growth. The appeal is low correlation to the cyclical and financial names bought the same day. Overhang risks are US drug-pricing policy and lingering litigation tails.

congress.rationale: Blackstone; the one US name in an otherwise international buy, adding alternative-asset-manager exposure.
congress.deepDive: Blackstone is the standout US name in an otherwise international basket, giving exposure to fee-earning AUM growth across private equity, credit and real estate. It's a leveraged play on a recovery in deal-making and fundraising, with a variable dividend tied to realizations. Its inclusion suggests a barbell: defensive dividend payers plus one higher-beta alternatives compounder. Risks are a prolonged commercial-real-estate drag and slower realizations in a higher-rate world.

congress.rationale: Iberdrola; regulated European utility / renewables, a defensive income holding.
congress.deepDive: Iberdrola is a regulated Spanish utility with a large renewables and grid-investment pipeline — a bond-proxy with a green-capex growth angle. It anchors the basket's defensive/income side and benefits from electrification and grid-upgrade spending across Europe. The trade-off is rate sensitivity (utilities de-rate when yields rise) and regulatory/tariff risk in its core markets.

congress.rationale: Coca-Cola FEMSA; EM consumer-staples bottler broadening geographic diversification.
congress.deepDive: Coca-Cola FEMSA is the largest Coke bottler, concentrated in Mexico and Latin America, adding emerging-market staples exposure with defensive volumes. It broadens the basket beyond Europe/US into LatAm consumption. The defensive demand profile is offset by FX translation risk (peso/real) and EM macro/political swings.

congress.rationale: BT Group; UK telecom value/yield play within the same international basket.
congress.deepDive: BT is a deep-value UK telecom with a high dividend and a multi-year fibre (Openreach) build that should inflect free cash flow as capex peaks. It's the most contrarian, turnaround-flavored line in the basket. Upside hinges on fibre monetization and cost cuts; risks are heavy debt, a large pension obligation, and UK competitive pricing.

congress.rationale: CNH Industrial; cyclical agricultural/construction equipment add rounding out the diversified spree.
congress.deepDive: CNH Industrial (agriculture and construction machinery) is the cyclical, early-recovery name in the basket — it adds beta to a global capex and farm-income upturn. Including one industrial cyclical alongside defensives and financials rounds out a balanced sector mix. The catch is the ag-equipment cycle is currently soft (lower crop prices, high dealer inventories), so this is an early/contrarian entry.

superInvestors.name: Berkshire Hathaway
superInvestors.rationale: Roughly tripled the Alphabet stake, vaulting it to a top-5 holding — a rare large tech bet signaling conviction in AI/search at a reasonable valuation.
superInvestors.deepDive: Berkshire has historically been light on big tech outside Apple, so tripling Alphabet to a top-5 position is a notable conviction signal — likely a post-Buffett-era investment-manager (Combs/Weschler or Abel-blessed) decision. The logic: Alphabet trades at a discount to other mega-cap AI beneficiaries while owning Search, YouTube, Cloud and DeepMind, giving cheap optionality on AI monetization. It contrasts sharply with the simultaneous trimming of Apple, Bank of America and Chevron — Berkshire is rotating quality-tech exposure, not adding net risk. For you, it's a vote of confidence in large-cap AI/search at a 'reasonable' multiple, a counterpoint to chasing pure semis.

superInvestors.name: Berkshire Hathaway
superInvestors.rationale: Continued multi-quarter trimming of Bank of America, reducing financial-sector and single-name concentration.
superInvestors.deepDive: This is the latest in a long sequence of BofA sales stretching back several quarters, steadily cutting what was once Berkshire's #2 holding. The motivation reads as de-risking concentrated financial exposure and harvesting gains at full valuations, plus possible tax/positioning ahead of rate cuts that pressure bank net interest margins. Paired with the Chevron and Apple trims, it shows a defensive, cash-building posture. Read-through: a cautious stance on US banks' near-term earnings — relevant context for your DBS/SGX-bank weight.

superInvestors.name: Berkshire Hathaway
superInvestors.rationale: Further trim of the largest holding (still ~22%), consistent with valuation discipline and locking in gains.
superInvestors.deepDive: Even after repeated trims Apple remains Berkshire's single biggest position (~22%), so this is valuation/risk management rather than a thesis change. Buffett has flagged Apple's rich multiple and the benefit of realizing gains while capital-gains rates are favorable. The trims feed Berkshire's record cash pile, leaving dry powder for a market dislocation. The signal is discipline, not abandonment — a reminder that even great businesses get trimmed on price.

superInvestors.name: Berkshire Hathaway
superInvestors.rationale: Sizable cut to Chevron as energy exposure is dialed back amid softer oil.
superInvestors.deepDive: Berkshire pared Chevron meaningfully as oil prices softened, reducing a position that had been a large energy/inflation hedge. It fits a broader 2026 Q1 pattern of trimming cyclicals and building cash. The move suggests less conviction in near-term energy upside, though Berkshire still retains substantial Occidental exposure. For commodity-tilted books, it's a mild caution flag on oil — distinct from precious metals, where you carry silver.

superInvestors.name: Berkshire Hathaway
superInvestors.rationale: Full exit as the portfolio was streamlined from 40 to 26 names and cash was built up.
superInvestors.deepDive: The Amazon stake was always small for Berkshire, so a full exit is part of housekeeping — concentrating the book from ~40 down to ~26 names. It rhymes with the Alphabet add: keep one high-conviction mega-cap platform (GOOGL), drop the marginal one (AMZN). The broader story is portfolio simplification plus a swelling cash balance, a posture that historically precedes Berkshire waiting for fatter pitches.

superInvestors.name: Berkshire Hathaway
superInvestors.rationale: Closed the UnitedHealth position amid managed-care headwinds and portfolio simplification.
superInvestors.deepDive: Exiting UnitedHealth removes exposure to a sector facing elevated medical-cost ratios, Medicare Advantage rate pressure and regulatory/political scrutiny. As a relatively new and small position, cutting it quickly suggests the original thesis didn't firm up. It aligns with the quarter's de-risking and name-count reduction. The read-through is caution on US managed care specifically.

superInvestors.name: Berkshire Hathaway
superInvestors.rationale: Exited Domino's, part of pruning smaller, non-core positions.
superInvestors.deepDive: Domino's was a minor position, and the exit is consistent with trimming the long tail of smaller holdings rather than a strong negative call. It contributes to the streamlining from 40 to 26 names. Not a market-moving signal on its own, but another data point in Berkshire's 'simplify and raise cash' quarter.

superInvestors.name: Pershing Square Capital Management
superInvestors.rationale: Ackman's brand-new Microsoft stake, funded by exiting Alphabet — a rotation into a higher-conviction AI/cloud compounder.
superInvestors.deepDive: Ackman opened Microsoft at roughly 15% of his highly concentrated book and funded it by selling all of Alphabet — a clear statement that he views MSFT (Azure + OpenAI + Copilot monetization across enterprise software) as the superior AI compounder. Pershing runs ~8-10 names, so a new top-tier position is a strong conviction signal. Interestingly this is the mirror image of Berkshire and Druckenmiller, who leaned into Alphabet — a genuine split among smart money on which mega-cap wins AI. Worth watching as a barometer for large-cap AI leadership.

superInvestors.name: Pershing Square Capital Management
superInvestors.rationale: Sold the entire Alphabet position to fund the new Microsoft holding.
superInvestors.deepDive: The full Alphabet exit directly financed the Microsoft initiation — a like-for-like rotation within mega-cap AI rather than a reduction in tech exposure. Ackman had held Alphabet through the AI-disruption-of-Search fears; cashing out now suggests he'd rather own the enterprise-software/cloud side of AI. The pair trade crystallizes his view that MSFT's monetization path is clearer than Google's.

superInvestors.name: Pershing Square Capital Management
superInvestors.rationale: Increased Amazon, keeping the book concentrated in mega-cap platform compounders (≈51% in top 3).
superInvestors.deepDive: Adding to Amazon pushes the top three positions to roughly half the portfolio, underscoring Pershing's concentrated, platform-compounder style. The thesis leans on AWS reacceleration, retail-margin expansion and advertising growth. Combined with the new MSFT stake, the book is now heavily levered to mega-cap cloud/AI — high conviction but also high single-theme concentration risk.

superInvestors.name: Pershing Square Capital Management
superInvestors.rationale: Closed the long-held Hilton position to recycle capital into higher-conviction ideas.
superInvestors.deepDive: Hilton was one of Ackman's longest-held, best-performing compounders, so exiting it is significant — it frees capital for the MSFT/AMZN tech tilt. The sale likely reflects a fully-valued asset-light lodging name plus a desire to concentrate into AI beneficiaries. It marks a stylistic shift from consumer/services compounders toward big tech.

superInvestors.name: Pershing Square Capital Management
superInvestors.rationale: Trimmed Brookfield, the largest holding, to fund the Microsoft initiation.
superInvestors.deepDive: Brookfield remained the largest position even after the trim, so this was a funding source for MSFT rather than a loss of conviction. Brookfield gives exposure to alternative-asset management, infrastructure and real assets. Trimming the winner to seed a new high-conviction idea is classic concentrated-portfolio capital recycling.

superInvestors.name: Duquesne Family Office (Stanley Druckenmiller)
superInvestors.rationale: New Broadcom stake adds AI-semiconductor exposure as he rotates out of mega-cap software.
superInvestors.deepDive: Druckenmiller initiated Broadcom for direct exposure to custom AI silicon (ASICs) and networking — arguably the 'picks and shovels' of the AI buildout — while cutting mega-cap software/ads names. AVGO's blend of AI compute, networking and sticky software (VMware) fits his macro-thematic, momentum-aware style. It signals he wants AI exposure closer to the hardware layer. Relevant tension for you: this favors semis over the broad software complex.

superInvestors.name: Duquesne Family Office (Stanley Druckenmiller)
superInvestors.rationale: Fresh stake in Caris Life Sciences, extending the portfolio's heavy healthcare-innovation/diagnostics tilt (NTRA is ~18-21%).
superInvestors.deepDive: Caris (molecular diagnostics/precision oncology) deepens an already large healthcare-innovation tilt anchored by Natera (~18-21% of the book). Druckenmiller is clearly building a basket around genomic diagnostics and personalized cancer care as a multi-year growth theme. These are higher-risk, clinical/commercial-stage names, so position sizing matters. It shows where a top macro investor sees secular growth outside of AI.

superInvestors.name: Duquesne Family Office (Stanley Druckenmiller)
superInvestors.rationale: New Revolution Medicines position, another bet on clinical-stage oncology innovation.
superInvestors.deepDive: Revolution Medicines is a clinical-stage oncology company (RAS-targeted cancer therapies), reinforcing the diagnostics-plus-therapeutics healthcare cluster. It's a binary, pipeline-driven name — upside on trial data, downside on setbacks — typically sized as part of a diversified innovation basket. Together with Caris and Natera it paints Druckenmiller's conviction in precision oncology as a durable theme.

superInvestors.name: Duquesne Family Office (Stanley Druckenmiller)
superInvestors.rationale: Fully exited Alphabet, mirroring a broader rotation away from mega-cap search/ads.
superInvestors.deepDive: The full Alphabet exit, alongside a near-total Amazon cut, marks a decisive rotation out of mega-cap ads/cloud into AI-hardware (AVGO) and healthcare. It's the opposite of Berkshire's Alphabet add — illustrating how differently top investors are positioning within tech. Druckenmiller tends to move fast on macro/momentum shifts, so this is a meaningful de-emphasis of the ad-driven platforms.

superInvestors.name: Duquesne Family Office (Stanley Druckenmiller)
superInvestors.rationale: Slashed Amazon by ~99%, sharply de-risking mega-cap tech exposure.
superInvestors.deepDive: Cutting Amazon by ~99% is effectively a thesis reversal on the name, leaving only a token stake. Combined with the Alphabet exit, Druckenmiller has stripped most mega-cap consumer-tech beta from the book in favor of AI semis and healthcare. The aggressiveness is characteristic — he sizes up and down hard on conviction. It hints at caution on consumer/cloud platforms' near-term risk/reward.

superInvestors.name: Duquesne Family Office (Stanley Druckenmiller)
superInvestors.rationale: Cut the Teva stake by ~60%, trimming a long-running generic-pharma value position.
superInvestors.deepDive: Teva had been a value/turnaround holding (deleveraging, biosimilars, branded pipeline); a ~60% cut suggests partial profit-taking or reduced conviction after a strong run. It's consistent with reallocating toward higher-growth healthcare-innovation names like Caris and Revolution. Not a full exit, so some residual constructive view remains.

superInvestors.name: Soros Fund Management LLC
superInvestors.rationale: Built Smurfit WestRock into the fund's largest single-stock holding — a packaging/industrials value and consolidation play.
superInvestors.deepDive: Smurfit WestRock (formed by the Smurfit Kappa–WestRock merger) is now Soros's largest single equity — a bet on packaging consolidation, synergy-driven margin expansion and a cyclical recovery in containerboard demand. It's a value/special-situations posture typical of the fund. Making it the top holding signals real conviction in the merger integration. Risks are industrial demand softness and integration execution.

superInvestors.name: Soros Fund Management LLC
superInvestors.rationale: Among 100+ new positions opened as the $9.1B book broadened; a defensive, cash-rich quality anchor.
superInvestors.deepDive: Adding Berkshire Hathaway gives the fund a defensive, cash-rich, diversified anchor as it broadened to 100+ new positions on a ~$9.1B book. It's a low-maintenance way to hold quality and dry powder via Buffett's record cash pile. The broad position count suggests a more diversified, less concentrated stance than peers. Effectively Soros is renting Berkshire's optionality on a market dislocation.

superInvestors.name: Soros Fund Management LLC
superInvestors.rationale: New regulated-utility position, adding defensive, rate-sensitive income to a diversified rebuild.
superInvestors.deepDive: WEC Energy is a regulated Midwest utility — a defensive, bond-proxy income holding that benefits if rates ease. Its addition fits a diversified, somewhat defensive rebuild of the book. Utilities also carry a quiet data-center/electrification demand tailwind. The main sensitivity is interest rates and regulatory rate-case outcomes.

superInvestors.name: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation Trust
superInvestors.rationale: Sold its last Microsoft shares, ending a 25-year holding and completing a multi-year diversification of the endowment away from its founding stock.
superInvestors.deepDive: The Trust sold its final ~7.7M Microsoft shares (~$3.2B), closing a position that traces back to Gates's founding stock and dwarfed the endowment for decades. This is governance/diversification-driven — reducing single-stock concentration risk for a perpetual charitable endowment — not a market call on Microsoft. It does, however, remove a large structural holder. The capital is being redeployed into a broader, more diversified mix to fund grant obligations.

superInvestors.name: Yorkville Advisors (DJT institutional holder)
superInvestors.rationale: Increased Trump Media & Technology stake even as DJT posted heavy losses; DJT remains majority-owned by the Donald J. Trump Revocable Trust, so float moves are dominated by a small institutional base.
superInvestors.deepDive: Yorkville added ~9.6% to its Trump Media (DJT) stake despite the company's heavy operating losses and tiny revenue — a sentiment/momentum-driven position rather than a fundamentals call. DJT is majority-owned by the Donald J. Trump Revocable Trust, so the public float is thin and dominated by a handful of institutions, which makes the stock highly volatile and headline-sensitive. Treat institutional 'adds' here as flow/positioning signals, not valuation endorsements. It's the closest public proxy to a 'Trump-linked' equity, hence its inclusion on the watch list.

insiders.rationale: CEO trimmed her stake shortly after an upbeat Q1 FY2026 report (released 30 Apr) as DBS shares recrossed S$60 — likely routine diversification/profit-taking rather than a directional signal.
insiders.deepDive: DBS CEO Tan Su Shan sold ~100,000 shares in May, shortly after a solid Q1 FY2026 result and as the stock recrossed S$60. CEO sales right after a strong print and into price strength are most often routine — diversification, tax, or vesting-related liquidity — rather than a bearish signal, especially when the executive retains a large remaining stake. Context matters for you: DBS is one of your single largest listed holdings (~S$191k), so it's worth watching whether other directors also sell (a cluster would be more meaningful than one sale). On its own this looks like normal profit-taking near a high, not a red flag.
